claim: Human ZDHHC6 is controlled by an upstream palmitoyltransferase, ZDHHC16.
source: Here we show that human ZDHHC6, which modifies key proteins of the endoplasmic reticulum, is controlled by an upstream palmitoyltransferase, ZDHHC16, revealing the first palmitoylation cascade.
evidence: Supported by siRNA screening, overexpression experiments, and knockout cell line analysis showing ZDHHC16 is responsible for ZDHHC6 palmitoylation.

claim: The ZDHHC16-ZDHHC6 system represents the first palmitoylation cascade.
source: Here we show that human ZDHHC6, which modifies key proteins of the endoplasmic reticulum, is controlled by an upstream palmitoyltransferase, ZDHHC16, revealing the first palmitoylation cascade.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding in the abstract and introduction, representing the first documented case of one palmitoyltransferase modifying another.

claim: ZDHHC6 has three palmitoylation sites in its SH3_2 domain.
source: Palmitoylation of ZDHHC6 was reported in two large-scale proteomics analysis to occur on Cys-328, Cys-329 and Cys-343 in the SH3 domain (Collins et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to proteomics studies and confirmed by mutagenesis experiments showing all three sites can be palmitoylated.

claim: ZDHHC6 can exist in eight differentially palmitoylated species based on occupancy of three palmitoylation sites.
source: The presence of 3 palmitoylation sites leads to the potential existence of 8 species: from fully unoccupied Cys-sites, noted C000, to full occupancy, noted C111, in the order of Cys-328, Cys-329 and Cys-343 in the exponent (Figure 5A).
evidence: Mathematical modeling and experimental data support the existence of these eight species with different properties.

claim: Each ZDHHC6 palmitoylation species varies in terms of turnover rate and activity.
source: We found that species rapidly interconvert through the action of ZDHHC16 and the Acyl Protein Thioesterase APT2, that each species varies in terms of turnover rate and activity, altogether allowing the cell to robustly tune its ZDHHC6 activity.
evidence: Demonstrated through pulse-chase experiments, activity assays with different mutants, and mathematical modeling predictions.

claim: APT2 mediates depalmitoylation of ZDHHC6.
source: Overexpression of WT, but not palmitoylation deficient, APT2 led to a significant decrease in ZDHHC6 palmitoylation. APT2S121A had an intermediate effect, possibly due to the formation of heterodimers between mutant and endogenous APT2 (Kong et al., 2013; Vujic et al., 2016). These observations show that ZDHHC6 palmitoylation is dynamic, in particular on Cys-328, and that depalmitoylation is mediated by APT2.
evidence: Supported by overexpression experiments showing APT2, but not APT1, affects ZDHHC6 palmitoylation levels.

claim: Palmitoylation of Cys-328 accelerates ZDHHC6 turnover.
source: Remarkably, mutation of Cys-328, but not of Cys-329 or Cys-343, abolished the sensitivity to ZDHHC16 overexpression or LYPLA2 silencing (Figure 3BC, Figure 1—figure supplement 1BC). LYPLA2 silencing led to ubiquitination of ZDHHC6 (Figure 3D) and ZDHHC6 degradation could be rescued by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 3E). Thus altogether these observations indicate that palmitoylation of Cys-328 renders ZDHHC6 susceptible to degradation by the ERAD pathway.
evidence: Demonstrated by metabolic pulse-chase experiments showing accelerated degradation upon ZDHHC16 overexpression or APT2 silencing, which is abolished in C328A mutant.

claim: Palmitoylation of Cys-328 renders ZDHHC6 susceptible to degradation by the ERAD pathway.
source: LYPLA2 silencing led to ubiquitination of ZDHHC6 (Figure 3D) and ZDHHC6 degradation could be rescued by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 3E). Thus altogether these observations indicate that palmitoylation of Cys-328 renders ZDHHC6 susceptible to degradation by the ERAD pathway.
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination assays and proteasome inhibitor rescue experiments.

claim: ZDHHC6 modifies calnexin, gp78, IP3 receptor, and transferrin receptor.
source: Here we focused on one of the 23 human palmitoyltransferase, ZDHHC6, which localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and controls a panel of key ER substrates such as the ER chaperone calnexin (Lakkaraju et al., 2012), the ER E3 ligase gp78 (Fairbank et al., 2012), the IP3 receptor (Fredericks et al., 2014) as well as cell surface proteins such as the transferrin receptor (Senyilmaz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by Acyl-RAC experiments in ZDHHC6 KO cells.

claim: Calnexin and transferrin receptor are exclusively modified by ZDHHC6.
source: Interestingly calnexin and Trf-R were no longer captured by Acyl-RAC in the HAP1 ZDHHC6 KO cells, confirming that they are exclusively modified by ZDHHC6, while capture of the IP3 receptor and gp78 was reduced but not abolished indicating that they can also be modified by other palmitoyltransferases (Figure 1B) consistent with previous findings (Fairbank et al., 2012; Fredericks et al., 2014).
evidence: Demonstrated by complete loss of palmitoylation signal in ZDHHC6 KO cells for these substrates.

claim: IP3 receptor and gp78 can be modified by palmitoyltransferases other than ZDHHC6.
source: Interestingly calnexin and Trf-R were no longer captured by Acyl-RAC in the HAP1 ZDHHC6 KO cells, confirming that they are exclusively modified by ZDHHC6, while capture of the IP3 receptor and gp78 was reduced but not abolished indicating that they can also be modified by other palmitoyltransferases (Figure 1B) consistent with previous findings (Fairbank et al., 2012; Fredericks et al., 2014).
evidence: Shown by partial retention of palmitoylation signal in ZDHHC6 KO cells and supported by previous literature.

claim: ZDHHC6 itself undergoes palmitoylation.
source: When probing samples for ZDHHC6, we found that the palmitoyltransferase itself was captured by Acyl-RAC in HAP1 cells (Figure 1B) and also in different mouse tissues (shown for mouse lung tissue in Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Acyl-RAC capture and 3H-palmitate incorporation experiments.

claim: ZDHHC6 does not autopalmitoylate itself.
source: WT and (∆DHHC) ZDHHC6 both underwent palmitoylation when transiently expressed in control or shRNA ZDHHC6 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that ZDHHC6 must be modified by another enzyme.
evidence: Shown by palmitoylation of catalytically inactive ZDHHC6 mutant and palmitoylation in ZDHHC6 knockdown cells.

claim: ZDHHC16 silencing leads to a 60% drop in ZDHHC6 palmitoylation.
source: We next performed 3H-palmitate labelling experiments upon siRNA silencing of each of the 23 DHHC enzymes. While a significant but mild drop was observed for several DHHC enzymes, only silencing of ZDHHC16 led to a major, 60%, drop in signal intensity (Figure 2A).
evidence: Quantified from siRNA screening experiments with 3H-palmitate labeling.

claim: All three ZDHHC6 palmitoylation sites are modified by ZDHHC16.
source: 3H-palmitate incorporation was also reduced for the AAC and CCA mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), showing that all three sites are modified by the same enzyme.
evidence: Demonstrated by reduced palmitoylation of all single and double cysteine mutants upon ZDHHC16 silencing.

claim: ZDHHC6 and ZDHHC16 can physically interact.
source: Consistent with these findings, co-immunoprecipitation experiments following transient over-expression of myc-tagged ZDHHC6 and FLAG-tagged ZDHHC16 showed that the two enzymes can interact (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: ZDHHC6 silencing or knockout leads to an increase in ZDHHC16 mRNA.
source: Interestingly, ZDHHC6 silencing in HeLa cells or ZDHHC6 knock out in HAP1 cells both led to an increase in the ZDHHC16 mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2AB), indicating that these two proteins interact physically and genetically.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative RT-PCR analysis in ZDHHC6 knockdown and knockout cells.

claim: ZDHHC16 is not palmitoylated in HeLa cells.
source: ZDHHC16, which localizes under over-expression conditions to the ER and the Golgi (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), is not palmitoylated itself in HeLa cells, as shown both by 3H-palmitate incorporation and Acyl-RAC (Figure 2—figure supplement 2BC).
evidence: Demonstrated by lack of 3H-palmitate incorporation and Acyl-RAC capture.

claim: 50% of palmitate is lost from ZDHHC6 in approximately 1 hour.
source: Following a 2 hr pulse, 50% of the 3H-palmitate was lost from ZDHHC6 in ≈1 hr, indicating rapid turnover of the acyl chains (Figure 2D).
evidence: Measured by 3H-palmitate pulse-chase experiments.

claim: Rapid palmitate turnover on ZDHHC6 requires the presence of Cys-328.
source: We performed similar experiments on the various single and double cysteine mutants and found that rapid turnover required the presence of Cys-328. In its absence, the apparent palmitate release rates were considerably slower, reaching more than 4 hr (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments on cysteine mutants showing slower depalmitoylation when Cys-328 is mutated.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type APT2 leads to a significant decrease in ZDHHC6 palmitoylation.
source: In contrast, overexpression of WT, but not palmitoylation deficient, APT2 led to a significant decrease in ZDHHC6 palmitoylation.
evidence: Shown by 3H-palmitate incorporation experiments with APT2 overexpression.

claim: APT1 overexpression has no detectable effect on ZDHHC6 palmitoylation.
source: Overexpression of WT or mutant APT1 had no detectable effect on ZDHHC6 palmitoylation (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Demonstrated by 3H-palmitate incorporation experiments showing no change with APT1 overexpression.

claim: Mutation of Cys-328 abolishes ZDHHC6 sensitivity to ZDHHC16 overexpression.
source: Remarkably, mutation of Cys-328, but not of Cys-329 or Cys-343, abolished the sensitivity to ZDHHC16 overexpression or LYPLA2 silencing (Figure 3BC, Figure 1—figure supplement 1BC).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments showing C328A mutant is not affected by ZDHHC16 overexpression.

claim: LYPLA2 silencing leads to ubiquitination of ZDHHC6.
source: LYPLA2 silencing led to ubiquitination of ZDHHC6 (Figure 3D) and ZDHHC6 degradation could be rescued by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Shown by immunoprecipitation and Western blotting with anti-ubiquitin antibodies.

claim: ZDHHC6 degradation can be rescued by the proteasome inhibitor MG132.
source: LYPLA2 silencing led to ubiquitination of ZDHHC6 (Figure 3D) and ZDHHC6 degradation could be rescued by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing increased ZDHHC6 levels upon MG132 treatment.

claim: Wild-type ZDHHC6 localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Ectopically expressed WT myc-ZDHHC6 shows a typical ER staining, co-localizing with Bip, a lumenal ER chaperone, and BAP31, a transmembrane ER protein (Figure 4AB), as did all the cysteine mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence colocalization with ER markers Bip and BAP31.

claim: The ZDHHC6 AAA mutant accumulates more frequently in dot-like ER structures compared to wild-type.
source: The ZDHHC6 AAA mutant was also clearly present in the reticular ER, but it tended to accumulate more frequently in dot-like ER structures, which stained positive for BAP31 but not Bip (Figure 4AB).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy and quantification of cells with dots.

claim: Palmitoylation affects ZDHHC6 localization within the ER membrane.
source: Thus the inability of ZDHHC6 AAA to undergo palmitoylation influences its localization within the two dimensional space of the ER membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the differential localization patterns of wild-type versus AAA mutant ZDHHC6.

claim: Wild-type ZDHHC6 can associate with itself.
source: Immunoprecipitation experiments using ZDHHC6 constructs with two different tags showed that WT ZDHHC6 can associate with itself as well as with the ∆DHHC variant but not with the AAA mutant (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with differentially tagged ZDHHC6 constructs.

claim: ZDHHC6 AAA mutant does not associate with wild-type ZDHHC6.
source: Immunoprecipitation experiments using ZDHHC6 constructs with two different tags showed that WT ZDHHC6 can associate with itself as well as with the ∆DHHC variant but not with the AAA mutant (Figure 4C).
evidence: Shown by lack of co-immunoprecipitation between wild-type and AAA mutant.

claim: ZDHHC6 can associate into higher order structures.
source: Blue native gel analysis confirmed that ZDHHC6 can associate into higher order structures, which could be dimers and above, or associate with detergent resistant membrane domains (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by blue native PAGE showing ZDHHC6 migrating at higher molecular weights.

claim: The AAA mutant forms higher order complexes that are different from those formed by wild-type ZDHHC6.
source: The AAA mutant also migrated as higher order complexes but these were clearly different from those formed by the WT protein (Figure 4D).
evidence: Shown by different migration patterns on blue native gels.

claim: Palmitoylation affects ZDHHC6 assembly into complexes or association with membrane domains.
source: Thus palmitoylation affects localization of ZDHHC6 in the ER as well as its assembly into complexes or association with membrane domains.
evidence: Inferred from the different complex formation patterns of wild-type versus AAA mutant on blue native gels.

claim: Calnexin palmitoylation is significantly reduced in ZDHHC16 KO cells.
source: Calnexin palmitoylation was significantly reduced in ZDHHC16 KO cells, as monitored by Acyl-RAC (Figure 4E) and enhanced upon ZDHHC16 over-expression (Figure 4F) indicating that palmitoylation indeed modulates ZDHHC6 activity.
evidence: Demonstrated by Acyl-RAC assay in ZDHHC16 knockout cells.

claim: ZDHHC16 overexpression enhances calnexin palmitoylation.
source: Calnexin palmitoylation was significantly reduced in ZDHHC16 KO cells, as monitored by Acyl-RAC (Figure 4E) and enhanced upon ZDHHC16 over-expression (Figure 4F) indicating that palmitoylation indeed modulates ZDHHC6 activity.
evidence: Shown by 3H-palmitate incorporation into calnexin upon ZDHHC16 overexpression.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type ZDHHC6 leads to 2.6 to 3-fold increase in calnexin and transferrin receptor palmitoylation.
source: Over-expression of WT ZDHHC6 led to 2.6 to 3-fold increase in calnexin and transferrin receptor palmitoylation, respectively (Figure 4GH).
evidence: Quantified from 3H-palmitate incorporation experiments.

claim: Overexpression of ZDHHC6 AAA has no effect on calnexin or transferrin receptor palmitoylation.
source: Overexpression of ZDHHC6 AAA had no effect on either target, confirming the importance of palmitoylation for ZDHHC6 activity.
evidence: Shown by 3H-palmitate incorporation experiments showing no increase in substrate palmitoylation.

claim: Palmitoylation of Cys-328 confers the highest activity to ZDHHC6.
source: The fact that palmitoylation of both ZDHHC6 targets is similarly affected by cysteine mutations rules out the possibility that differentially palmitoylated ZDHHC6 molecules could have different target specificities. Together these experiments indicate that palmitoylation of Cys-328 confers the highest activity to ZDHHC6.
evidence: Demonstrated by activity assays showing mutants lacking Cys-328 have reduced ability to palmitoylate substrates.

claim: The C000 species of ZDHHC6 is predicted to have a half-life of approximately 40 hours.
source: C000 is predicted to have a half-life of approx. 40 hr (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 2A), consistent with the decay measured experimentally for the AAA triple mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Predicted by mathematical modeling and validated by experimental measurements of AAA mutant.

claim: The major palmitoylation and depalmitoylation fluxes occur between C000 and C100.
source: The major fluxes through the system are from C000 to C100, backwards, corresponding to palmitoylation and depalmitoylation of Cys-328 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Determined by flux analysis from the mathematical model.

claim: In tissue culture cells, approximately 70% of ZDHHC6 is non-palmitoylated at steady state.
source: Estimation of the steady state distribution of species indicated that in experimental setting –HeLa cells in culture– the ZDHHC6 cellular population is about 70% non-palmitoylated and 20% palmitoylated, the most abundant species being C010 and C011 (Figure 5F).
evidence: Predicted by mathematical modeling and confirmed by PEGylation assay showing only non-palmitoylated form is detectable.

claim: Each ZDHHC6 molecule undergoes multiple rounds of palmitoylation-depalmitoylation during its life cycle.
source: The model altogether predicts that in tissue culture HeLa cells, each ZDHHC6 molecule undergoes multiple rounds of palmitoylation-depalmitoylation during its life cycle mostly on Cys-328.
evidence: Predicted by stochastic simulations showing average of 2.7 passages through C100 state per molecule.

claim: ZDHHC6 molecules spend most of their time in the C000 state.
source: ZDHHC6 molecules were predicted to spend most of their time, by far, in the C000 state (Figure 5E).
evidence: Predicted by stochastic single molecule tracking simulations.

claim: At any given time, approximately 60% of ZDHHC6 molecules are not acylated in tissue culture cells.
source: At any given time, approximately 60% of the molecules are not acylated.
evidence: Predicted by mathematical modeling of steady state distribution.

claim: ZDHHC16 overexpression leads to C011 becoming the most abundant ZDHHC6 species.
source: ZDHHC16 overexpression led to a major shift in species distribution, C011 then representing 60% of the population (Figure 6A).
evidence: Predicted by mathematical modeling under ZDHHC16 overexpression conditions.

claim: ZDHHC16 overexpression leads to only a 15% drop in overall ZDHHC6 content.
source: Interestingly, the overall ZDHHC6 content dropped by only 15% (Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: Predicted by mathematical modeling and confirmed experimentally by Western blot.

claim: LYPLA2 silencing leads to a 72% drop in ZDHHC6 content.
source: Lypla2 silencing in contrast led to a 72% drop in ZDHHC6 content (Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: Predicted by mathematical modeling and confirmed experimentally.

claim: The CAA mutant cellular content is predicted to be 84% of wild-type under control conditions.
source: Under control conditions, the total CAA content is predicted to be 84% of WT, and mostly in the non-palmitoylated state (Figure 6B).
evidence: Predicted by mathematical modeling.

claim: The CAA mutant cellular content drops to 32% of wild-type upon ZDHHC16 overexpression.
source: The CAA cellular content is however predicted to drop to 32% of WT control levels upon ZDHHC16 overexpression (Figure 6B).
evidence: Predicted by mathematical modeling and confirmed experimentally by Western blot showing 60% drop.

claim: The presence of 3 palmitoylation sites renders ZDHHC6 protein content robust to changes in ZDHHC16 activity.
source: All together, these predictions suggest that the presence of 3 palmitoylation sites, as opposed to just Cys-328, renders the ZDHHC6 protein content robust to changes in ZDHHC16 activity.
evidence: Inferred from modeling predictions showing wild-type is more stable than CAA mutant upon ZDHHC16 overexpression.

claim: Upon ZDHHC16 overexpression, all ZDHHC6 molecules explore all palmitoylation states.
source: Stochastic simulations predicted that overexpression of ZDHHC16 would drastically increase the dynamics of the network (Figure 6C vs. Figure 5E). Indeed, all ZDHHC6 molecules explored all the palmitoylation states, with extremely short residence times in each (Figure 6C).
evidence: Predicted by stochastic simulations under ZDHHC16 overexpression conditions.

claim: C011 is the hub of the ZDHHC6 palmitoylation system when ZDHHC16 activity is high.
source: When analysing 10'000 simulations, 22'000 events of palmitoylation-depalmitoylation emanated from C011 whereas only 4'000 events occurred between C000 and C100. Thus when activity of ZDHHC16 is high, C011 appears to be the hub of the system.
evidence: Determined by analysis of stochastic simulations counting transition events.

claim: C011 has the slowest turnover rate of all ZDHHC6 species.
source: C011 has the slowest turover rate of all ZDHHC6 species, explaining why the protein levels are stable.
evidence: Predicted by mathematical modeling showing long half-life for C011.

claim: Wild-type ZDHHC6 protein levels do not drastically drop upon ZDHHC16 overexpression.
source: Western blot analysis of protein abundance showed that WT ZDHHC6 protein levels drastically dropped upon siRNA of Lypla2 (Figure 4B), but not upon ZDHHC16 overexpression (Figure 6DE).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification.

claim: ZDHHC16 overexpression leads to a 60% drop in CAA mutant expression.
source: ZDHHC16 overexpression however led to a 60% drop in CAA expression (Figure 6DE).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification.

claim: AAA mutant expression is not affected by ZDHHC16 overexpression.
source: As expected, expression of AAA was not affected (Figure 6DE).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis.

claim: ZDHHC16 overexpression enhances the ability of wild-type ZDHHC6 to modify calnexin.
source: The ability of WT ZDHHC6 to modify calnexin was enhanced by ZDHHC16 overexpression (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by 3H-palmitate incorporation into calnexin.

claim: ZDHHC16 overexpression reduces calnexin palmitoylation to background levels in CAA ZDHHC6 expressing cells.
source: In contrast, ZDHHC16 overexpression reduced calnexin palmitoylation to background levels in CAA ZDHHC6 expressing cells (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by 3H-palmitate incorporation into calnexin showing loss of activity.

claim: ZDHHC6 is more palmitoylated in mouse tissues than in tissue culture cells.
source: When ZDHHC6 PEGylation experiments were performed on different mouse tissues, we however found that ZDHHC6 is far more palmitoylated, suggesting that palmitoylation-mediated ZDHHC6 activity is higher in vivo, a situation that we could mimic in cells by ZDHHC16 overexpression.
evidence: Demonstrated by PEGylation assays showing multiple palmitoylated species in mouse tissues.

claim: ZDHHC6 is mainly in the non-palmitoylated form in HeLa cells under control tissue culture conditions.
source: The above experimental analyses show that in HeLa cells under control tissue culture conditions, ZDHHC6 is mainly in the non-palmitoylated form.
evidence: Demonstrated by PEGylation assay showing only non-palmitoylated band detectable.

claim: ZDHHC9 requires a co-factor, GCP16, for activity.
source: DHHC9 was found to require a co-factor, GCP16, for activity (Swarthout et al., 2005), as also found in yeast (Lobo et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ZDHHC6 was proposed to require Selenoprotein K to function.
source: Similarly, ZDHHC6 was proposed to require Selenoprotein K to function (Fredericks and Hoffmann, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In the non-palmitoylated form, ZDHHC6 has no detectable activity.
source: Here we show that ZDHHC6 activity is controlled by palmitoylation in its C-terminal SH3_2-domain. In the non-palmitoylated form, ZDHHC6 has no detectable activity.
evidence: Demonstrated by activity assays showing AAA mutant has no effect on substrate palmitoylation.

claim: ZDHHC16 is essential for embryonic and postnatal survival in mice.
source: ZDHHC16/Aph2 is essential for embryonic and postnatal survival, eye and heart development in mice (Zhou et al., 2015), for the proliferation of neural stem cells, where it is involved in the activation of the FGF/erk pathways (Shi et al., 2016) and was reported to play a role in DNA damage response (Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: ZDHHC16 is involved in eye and heart development in mice.
source: ZDHHC16/Aph2 is essential for embryonic and postnatal survival, eye and heart development in mice (Zhou et al., 2015), for the proliferation of neural stem cells, where it is involved in the activation of the FGF/erk pathways (Shi et al., 2016) and was reported to play a role in DNA damage response (Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: ZDHHC16 is involved in the proliferation of neural stem cells.
source: ZDHHC16/Aph2 is essential for embryonic and postnatal survival, eye and heart development in mice (Zhou et al., 2015), for the proliferation of neural stem cells, where it is involved in the activation of the FGF/erk pathways (Shi et al., 2016) and was reported to play a role in DNA damage response (Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: ZDHHC16 is involved in the activation of the FGF/erk pathways.
source: ZDHHC16/Aph2 is essential for embryonic and postnatal survival, eye and heart development in mice (Zhou et al., 2015), for the proliferation of neural stem cells, where it is involved in the activation of the FGF/erk pathways (Shi et al., 2016) and was reported to play a role in DNA damage response (Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: ZDHHC16 plays a role in DNA damage response.
source: ZDHHC16/Aph2 is essential for embryonic and postnatal survival, eye and heart development in mice (Zhou et al., 2015), for the proliferation of neural stem cells, where it is involved in the activation of the FGF/erk pathways (Shi et al., 2016) and was reported to play a role in DNA damage response (Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: APT2 is involved in cell polarity-mediated tumor suppression.
source: APT2, which was recently found to be involved in cell polarity-mediated tumor suppression (Hernandez et al., 2017) but is otherwise poorly characterized, also undergoes palmitoylation by a yet to be determined palmitoyltransferase (Kong et al., 2013; Vartak et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: APT2 undergoes palmitoylation by a yet to be determined palmitoyltransferase.
source: APT2, which was recently found to be involved in cell polarity-mediated tumor suppression (Hernandez et al., 2017) but is otherwise poorly characterized, also undergoes palmitoylation by a yet to be determined palmitoyltransferase (Kong et al., 2013; Vartak et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DHHC enzymes are typically present in less than 1000 copies per cell.
source: According to large-scale quantitative proteomics analyses, DHHC enzymes are typically present in less than 1000 copies per cell (Beck et al., 2011; Foster et al., 2003; Nagaraj et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to proteomics studies.

claim: Calnexin is present in half a million to a million copies per cell.
source: Together this information indicates that, at any given time, tissue culture cells contain a very low number of active ZDHHC6 enzymes. In these cells, target proteins do however undergo palmitoylation, and some of these targets are highly abundant proteins such as calnexin (half a million to a million copies per cell [Beck et al., 2011; Foster et al., 2003; Nagaraj et al., 2011]).
evidence: Supported by citations to proteomics studies.

claim: When active, ZDHHC6 is a very potent enzyme.
source: Thus when active, ZDHHC6 appears be a very potent enzyme and our observations indicate that cells tend to avoid having too much of it.
evidence: Inferred from the low abundance of active ZDHHC6 yet efficient palmitoylation of abundant substrates like calnexin.

claim: Cells tend to avoid having too much active ZDHHC6.
source: Thus when active, ZDHHC6 appears be a very potent enzyme and our observations indicate that cells tend to avoid having too much of it. Indeed the C100 species of ZDHHC6 is either rapidly depalmitoylated or targeted to degradation via the ERAD pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the rapid turnover and degradation of the most active C100 species.

claim: ZDHHC6 can adopt three types of states: stable and inactive (C000), highly active and short-lived (C100), and moderately active and long-lived (C010 and C011).
source: Altogether this study indicates that ZDHHC6 can adopt in 3 types of states: 1) stable and inactive (C000); 2) highly active, short-lived and rapidly turned over (C100); 3) moderately active, long-lived and very slowly turned over (C010 and C011).
evidence: Inferred from the combined analysis of activity assays, degradation kinetics, and mathematical modeling.

claim: The regulatory system allows the cell to tightly control the activity of ZDHHC6.
source: Such a regulatory system allows the cell to tightly control the activity of ZDHHC6.
evidence: Inferred from the complex interplay between palmitoylation, depalmitoylation, activity, and degradation.

claim: Palmitoylation has a more subtle and precise effect than merely increasing hydrophobicity.
source: We found that depending on the site of modification both the activity and turnover of ZDHHC6 were strongly affected, indicating that palmitoylation has a more subtle and precise effect than merely increasing hydrophobicity, consistent with recent findings on single acylated species of Ras (Pedro et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from site-specific effects on activity and stability, supported by citation to similar findings in Ras.

claim: S-Palmitoylation is the only reversible post-translational lipid modification.
source: S-Palmitoylation is the only reversible post-translational lipid modification.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Palmitoylation may control the interaction of a protein with membranes or specific membrane domains.
source: More precisely, palmitoylation may control the interaction of a protein with membranes or specific membrane domains, affect its conformation, trafficking, stability and/or activity (Blaskovic et al., 2014; Chamberlain et al., 2013; Conibear and Davis, 2010; Fukata et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Palmitoylation may affect protein conformation, trafficking, stability and/or activity.
source: More precisely, palmitoylation may control the interaction of a protein with membranes or specific membrane domains, affect its conformation, trafficking, stability and/or activity (Blaskovic et al., 2014; Chamberlain et al., 2013; Conibear and Davis, 2010; Fukata et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles.

claim: In the cytosol, the acyl chain is attached to the protein via a thioester bond through the action of DHHC palmitoyltransferases.
source: In the cytosol, the acyl chain is attached to the protein via a thioester bond through the action of DHHC palmitoyltransferases, a family of multispanning transmembrane proteins (Blaskovic et al., 2014; Chamberlain et al., 2013; Conibear and Davis, 2010; Fukata et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles.

claim: There are 23 human palmitoyltransferases.
source: Here we focused on one of the 23 human palmitoyltransferase, ZDHHC6, which localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and controls a panel of key ER substrates such as the ER chaperone calnexin (Lakkaraju et al., 2012), the ER E3 ligase gp78 (Fairbank et al., 2012), the IP3 receptor (Fredericks et al., 2014) as well as cell surface proteins such as the transferrin receptor (Senyilmaz et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: ZDHHC6 is a tetra-spanning membrane protein.
source: As most DHHC enzymes, ZDHHC6 is a tetra-spanning membrane protein.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about DHHC enzyme structure.

claim: ZDHHC6 has a short N-terminal extension and a long C-terminal tail.
source: It has a short N-terminal extension and a long C-terminal tail composed of an approximately 100-residue domain of unknown structure followed by a variant SH3_2 domain (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Described based on sequence analysis and shown in figures.

claim: The KKNR motif contributes to the ER localization of ZDHHC6.
source: At the C-terminus, it contains a KKNR motif which when transferred to the ZDHHC3 enzyme leads to its relocalization from the Golgi to the ER (Gorleku et al., 2011), suggesting that it contributes to the ER localization of ZDHHC6.
evidence: Inferred from previous study showing this motif can relocalize ZDHHC3 to ER.

claim: The palmitoylated cysteines in ZDHHC6 are conserved in vertebrates.
source: These cysteines are conserved in vertebrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by sequence alignment in figure supplement.

claim: ZDHHC16 localizes to the ER and the Golgi under overexpression conditions.
source: ZDHHC16, which localizes under over-expression conditions to the ER and the Golgi (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), is not palmitoylated itself in HeLa cells, as shown both by 3H-palmitate incorporation and Acyl-RAC (Figure 2—figure supplement 2BC).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: ZDHHC16 is also known as Ablphilin 2 (Aph2).
source: ZDHHC16, also known as Ablphilin 2 (Aph2), is, as ZDHHC6, expressed in many human tissues in particular in the heart, pancreas, liver, skeletal muscle (Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated as established nomenclature with citation.

claim: ZDHHC16 is expressed in many human tissues, particularly in the heart, pancreas, liver, and skeletal muscle.
source: ZDHHC16, also known as Ablphilin 2 (Aph2), is, as ZDHHC6, expressed in many human tissues in particular in the heart, pancreas, liver, skeletal muscle (Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: ZDHHC16 can interact with the non-receptor tyrosine kinase c-Abl at the ER surface.
source: Its name Ablphilin stems from its ability to interact with the non-receptor tyrosine kinase c-Abl at the ER surface (Li et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: HAP1 ZDHHC6 KO clone contains a 5 bp deletion in exon 2.
source: The ZDHHC6 clone (13474–01) contains a 5 bp deletion in exon 2 (NM_022494) and the ZDHHC16 clone (36523–06) contains a 2 bp insertion in exon 2 (NM_198043).
evidence: Described in the methods section as characterization of the knockout cell line.

claim: HAP1 ZDHHC16 KO clone contains a 2 bp insertion in exon 2.
source: The ZDHHC6 clone (13474–01) contains a 5 bp deletion in exon 2 (NM_022494) and the ZDHHC16 clone (36523–06) contains a 2 bp insertion in exon 2 (NM_198043).
evidence: Described in the methods section as characterization of the knockout cell line.

claim: The model was calibrated using 152 parameter sets selected from genetic algorithm optimization.
source: From the Pareto set provided by the GA and in order to be more accurate and to reduce the variability in the output of the model, we selected the set of parameters that best fitted the calibration data. The procedure for the selection of the subset is described in (Dallavilla et al., 2016). In total, 152 different sets of parameter were selected at the end of the optimization.
evidence: Described in the methods section for model parameterization.

claim: The number of ZDHHC6 molecules per HeLa cell is in the order of 1600 molecules.
source: A single assumption was added to those previously defined (Dallavilla et al., 2016), namely that the number of ZDHHC6 molecules per HeLa cell is in the order of 1600 molecules (Beck et al., 2011; Merrick et al., 2011; Nagaraj et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2010; Yount et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on citations to proteomics studies.
